verses.note: The church fathers often read "Let Us" as a first glimpse of the Trinity. Most interpreters today agree the first readers would not have heard it that way, but many still think it fitting that the fuller revelation of Father, Son, and Spirit makes sense of the plural. The verse does not prove the doctrine; the doctrine rests on the New Testament.

The Trinitarian reading of verse 24 has an ancient history in Christian interpretation, but most modern commentators, Christian and Jewish, see a Hebrew stylistic repetition. The doctrine of the Trinity rests on the New Testament, not on this verse.

The New Testament writers keep the Shema and confess Jesus within it. Paul's ‘one God, the Father’ and ‘one Lord, Jesus Christ’ (1 Corinthians 8:6) divides the Shema's own words between Father and Son. The church's doctrine of the Trinity is a confession of the one God of this verse, not a departure from it.

Christian theology read ‘begotten’ as describing the Son's eternal relation to the Father, the language the Nicene Creed uses (‘begotten, not made’). The psalm does not state that doctrine on its own; it supplies the vocabulary of Father and Son that the fuller revelation fills.

The one addressed as God in verse 6 has a God in verse 7 who anoints him. Christian theology, following Hebrews 1:9, reads the pair as the Son addressed by the Father; Acts 10:38 speaks of God anointing Jesus with the Holy Spirit. The verse does not by itself teach the doctrine, but it is one of the Old Testament lines the early church found it could only read in that light.
Before the baptism scene, John already links the coming Son to the Spirit whom he will give. Mark's prologue introduces all three persons before Jesus says a word.
The Son rises from the water, the Spirit descends, and in the next verse the Father speaks. The church fathers pointed to this scene when they confessed one God in three persons.
The Father speaks to the Son on whom the Spirit has come. The New Testament does not yet use the word Trinity, but this scene became one of the church's principal witnesses to the three persons.

The verse holds two truths together that the church would later spell out as the doctrine of the Trinity: the Word is personally distinct from God the Father (with God) and shares the one divine nature (was God). Either claim without the other would deny what John says.

The relationship between the Word and God did not begin at the incarnation. It was there in the beginning, which is why the church confessed that the Son's relation to the Father is eternal, not a role he took on for a time.

The verse begins and ends the prologue's frame: the Son is God and is at the Father's side, as the Word was God and with God in verse 1. Distinction and oneness are held together at the close exactly as at the opening.
The Father who sent John speaks, the Spirit descends, and the Son is identified. The scene is one of the passages from which the church learned to confess one God in three persons.

The Father's love for the Son is the ground of the Son's authority. The relation between them is described as love before it is described as command, and the Gospel later says the Father loved the Son before the foundation of the world (17:24).

The Father gives the promised Spirit to the exalted Son, and the Son pours the Spirit out on his people. The verse names all three persons and their distinct roles in a single act, which later theology would describe as the Spirit sent by the Father through the Son.
